# DAY2 From "???" to "Aah, I get it!" It's little funny cause I come from an engineering background (although electrical hehe), so I have seen code many times before also. But back then, it was always like I had to do it for **exams** only. Today's class felt different. Maybe because it was connected to design, maybe because we were constantly seeing things happen *visually*, but it made coding feel much more approachable than I had imagined. There were definitely moments where my brain just froze trying to remember what each tag was doing. But once we started putting things together and seeing the structure build up, it slowly began to make sense. I realized it's less about memorizing everything and more about understanding how different pieces work together. Then I felt something that is like I do more often, it felt like filmmaking process. Like there is something called acting, cinematography, dialogue, etc those things and **html code** is same like that is a structure and content but then there are things like art direction, lighting, set design etc which is pretty similar to **CSS** part that where we style the frame. So, at the end I am happy that I am able to understand today's learning points. The physical website activity was honestly one of my favourite parts of the day. It's interesting how arranging pieces of paper and physically building a webpage made the whole idea click much faster than just looking at a screen. I always enjoy activities where I have to do some hands-on work! And then came the **ugly website**. I don't know why, but making something intentionally ugly was so much fun. I actually like maximalist and abstract style. And there was no pressure to make it look "good," so it just became one big experiment. I'd search for a random CSS property, try it out, refresh the page, laugh at whatever happened, and repeat. Sometimes I'd accidentally ruin the whole layout (*although that was the task no!*), sometimes I'd discover something unexpected that actually looked cool. It reminded me that experimenting without worrying about the outcome is probably one of the best ways to learn, I wish I could explain this to my clients... **CSS Diner** game was also super fun. It was more like trying to figure out the correct logic and it also helped for some CSS syntax too like how to style a particular class and all. Initially, it was little tough for me to crack down, but then like how Argentina played in the FIFA World Cup this year, I also got awake in last 10 minutes haha. One major learning for me today was that I saw website as a creative medium today rather than just a utility website, I mean yeah, it's a first day only but still I felt that as a designer this is also another tool like illustrator or something! Also, I am happy that I played football in the evening after a hectic work days of past 2 months, and hoping that I will be able to do everyday... Logging off with a film recommendation: **Kiki's Delivery Service** Cute, warm classic japanese anime movie!

### Ctrl + Panic Today's class had everything like fun discussions, little little victories, confusion (soooooo much of confusion), panic, and then some magical moments where the right thing gets clicked! The day started with a discussion, and I genuinely enjoy those sessions. I like how everyone thinks because the same topic somehow ends up with ten different perspectives. Sometimes someone says something that completely changes how I was thinking about it. The frog game was very addictive, honestly. It felt much easier than yesterday's game, but at the same time there was so much to learn that my brain was constantly processing something new. The best part was that it actually helped in the afternoon exercise. I could feel that I wasn't just randomly clicking anymore, I was understanding why something worked. But, but, but then came the afternoon task.... The first few levels were smooth, and I was feeling pretty confident. Then task 5 happened. _Fahhhhh..._ I spent almost half an hour just trying to understand the HTML structure. I wasn't even writing CSS at that point; I was just staring at the code trying to figure out what was happening. Then I suddenly remembered something Aman sir had mentioned in the morning. I opened Chrome's Inspect tool and started exploring the HTML from different websites there. That honestly changed everything. Instead of guessing, I could actually see the structure and understand what I was targeting. It felt like discovering a cheat code (the legal kind). Another tiny thing that made me unnecessarily happy, I realized how messy I had been writing my code till now. Everything was just... there. While struggling with task 5, I searched if there was a way to format code in VS Code, and apparently all it took was a right-click and Format Document. One click and everything became neat. I literally smiled at my screen. Coming from a design background where organizing things often means manually nudging every little element into place, this felt like a luxury. After that, the difficulty just kept increasing. Some selectors really made me question my life choices for a second. Thankfully, discussing with everyone around made a huge difference. Sometimes all it takes is one small hint, and suddenly the whole problem starts making sense. The nicest ending to the day was completing the bonus task by myself. It wasn't a huge achievement, but after all the confusion and debugging, it felt incredibly satisfying. The tiredness instantly disappeared. Now the only challenge left is sitting down tonight and making notes from everything we learnt today. That might actually be harder than today's exercises. My insomnia helps me to stay awake but with a little alzheimer's (not serious Alzheimer's though but yeah...) # Plot Twist in Process If someone asked me what this weekend felt like, I'd say it was like learning to ride a bicycle...except every five minutes someone was secretly removing one of the wheels. The storytelling website was an emotional rollercoaster. One moment I'd be sitting there thinking, "Okay...I think I am finally understanding HTML and CSS." The next moment, one tiny thing would refuse to work, and suddenly I was questioning the decisions that had brought me to that particular < div >. I don't think I have ever refreshed a browser this many times in my life. But honestly, that's what made it fun. Every bug had its own personality. Some got solved in thirty seconds, some took half an hour just because I forgot one tiny thing. The funniest part is that when it finally worked, I would just sit there staring at the screen like... "That's it? THAT was the problem?" Although, apart from working on this website, I also enjoyed the weekend; I watched 2 movies each day instead of one, I wrote my unfinished story, also I got a chance to start writing for a play, and then few freelance work, also also I played against NID and gladly scored a hat trick and won the match too hehehe, so it was a happy weekend. Today's clock project felt like entering a completely different universe because this time we were allowed to use an LLM. I really liked that thing which Aman Sir said, and later on I also felt it's true, like using the word 'LLM' instead of 'AI' surely changes the approach towards using it. I will admit, somewhere in my mind I thought, "Nice, this should be easy now," but reality was slightly different. Yes, it made things faster. But very quickly I realised that an LLM isn't a magician; it's more like that super-fast teammate who takes your instructions very quickly and literally. If I wrote a lazy prompt, it gave me a lazy result, and my credits got wasted. If I forgot to mention one tiny detail, it would still make something by itself happily. Hence, I understood that explaining what I actually want is also a skill in its own right. The weirdest realization came at the end of the day. I actually appreciated the storytelling website more after making the clock. Last week's struggles suddenly felt worth it. If I hadn't spent days fighting with HTML and CSS, I don't think I would've understood half of what the LLM was generating. Earlier I was asking, "Why isn't this working?" Today I was asking, "What's the exact error or part that is appearing here?" That's a much more exciting question to ask. Also, can we appreciate how dramatically my relationship with Inspect Element has changed? A few days ago it looked like some forbidden developer territory. Now I open it like I know exactly what I'm doing... (I don't. But confidence is important.) Debugging the error and understanding which exact part it is happening, this inspect tool really helped me a lot. Overall, it was a fun week, super fun weekend, and excited for this coming week that started today. Here I am clocking my submission in: [The Clock I tried to Make](https://cinematictime.netlify.app/) I will try to experiment with a few more concepts with the clock and add them here in this thread only in this note later Logging off with a film recommendation: The Social Network (2010)

devNotes.content: # Wait, I can make my own web space the way I want? You know that feeling when someone asks you a really simple question and suddenly your brain decides to overthink your entire existence? Yeah... today's question was basically, **"What is your website?"** I thought I'd have an answer in five minutes. Three hours later, I was imagining my website as a football pitch, then a film set, then my bookshelf, then my room, then a weird museum of random things I've collected over the years. Safe to say... things escalated quickly. The morning discussions were honestly my favourite part. I love those sessions because everyone somehow reads the same thing but walks away with completely different thoughts. One person notices the politics behind the web, another talks about digital gardens, someone else starts questioning social media, and I'm just sitting there collecting everyone's ideas like Pokemon cards alongside, putting out my Pokemon to play also! The blogs themselves were so refreshing. For the longest time, I've always thought of websites as either portfolios or company websites. That's it. But today I realized... who made that rule? Like, I always wanted to explore, but yeah never gathered the courage to. A website can literally be a place that grows with you. It doesn't have to look "finished." It doesn't have to be optimized for recruiters or algorithms or whoever keeps inventing these rules. It can just... exist. Like a garden. You keep planting things, some grow, some die, some look terrible, some unexpectedly become your favourite part. I think the biggest realization for me came today while writing my manifesto. I've always had this tiny guilt of liking too many things. Films, photography, football, design, books, music, writing, random observations, collecting old things... my brain never wants to stay in one lane. Every time someone asks, "So what's your niche?" my brain quietly replies, "...yes." But while looking at other people's websites today, especially one that was absolutely overflowing with journals, experiments, updates, tiny thoughts, old work, new work, and random collections, I didn't think, "This is too much." I thought, "Wait... I'm allowed to do this?" That was probably my favourite moment of the day. Instead of feeling like I have to remove parts of myself to make a "clean portfolio," I suddenly felt like maybe I should add more. Maybe my website shouldn't hide all the weird side quests I keep going on. Maybe that's the interesting part. By the end of the day, I wasn't thinking about layouts or navigation anymore. I was just excited. Not excited to make a website. Excited to slowly build a place that feels like me. In that excitement only, I kinda wrote too much? Or I don't know, but here is my Canva presentation link where I tried to put everything in a structured way. [Please Click Here Carefully!](https://canva.link/hdafn1cpwics2sm) (Also... I have a strong feeling this project is going to become way bigger than the assignment. Oops.)
